extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and informed public interested in the impact of AI on mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating what counts as good mathematics and how AI changes mathematical practice — including qualities of proofs, which problems are valued, and how verification and collaboration might evolve. The page is a journalistic overview of norms, concerns, and emerging workflows in math in the AI era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as a rigorous logical argument
rubrics_metrics.description: “The heart of mathematics has been the proof — a rigorous, logical argument for whether a given statement is true or false.” Mathematicians’ careers are measured by the theorems they can prove and how many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs should be step-by-step deductions built from axioms and lemmas; correctness (logical validity) is the primary baseline for mathematical work. The article frames proof as the defining standard of the field and the main metric by which mathematicians are evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance, creativity, and beauty of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best proofs are works of art. They’re not just rigorous; they’re elegant, creative and beautiful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond mere correctness, proofs are valued for explanatory clarity, conceptual insight, and aesthetic qualities; these human-valued aspects make proofs feel like creative work rather than only mechanical derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding and hands-on engagement with details
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians value getting “your hands dirty” as the source of understanding; many worry that outsourcing detail to AI could harm their ability to think and fully understand mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong criterion for mathematical practice is internalized understanding — not just having a verified proof on paper but knowing the details oneself. The article records concerns (e.g., Granville, Litt) that losing this engagement could negatively affect training and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal verification / machine-checkable proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs encoded in proof assistants (e.g., Lean) can be checked by software; fragments can be written by hand or generated by AI and then verified by a formal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal verification is presented as an operational standard for correctness: a proof that a program verifies is guaranteed to follow a valid chain of logic. The article notes that packaging steps into tactics and automated verification could allow outsourcing of routine detail while maintaining formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential separation between formal rigor and human comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A possible future where there is a “divorce between rigor on the paper and rigor in your head,” i.e., formal correctness exists but human understanding of every detail may be lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evaluative tension: a proof may be formally correct yet not be fully understood by humans; the article highlights this as both a practical possibility and an ideological concern among mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and importance of lemmas and foundational steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemmas are minor statements that must be proved true and combined to build larger proofs; they are often time-consuming, may require little creativity, yet are necessary bricks in a proof’s structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats automation of lemmas as a clear opportunity for AI: automating tedious lemmas could speed research and change what mathematicians focus on. Evaluations of proofs should therefore consider both the global blueprint and the correctness of foundational lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor and scalability through collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale mathematical projects (e.g., classification of finite simple groups, Terence Tao’s equational theories project) show that many contributors can collectively accomplish results no individual could.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion for modern mathematical work, the ability to coordinate specialized roles (theorists, verifiers, translators to machine language, explainers) and to manage large collaborative efforts will be important. The article suggests that AI will accelerate such division of labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance and taste-driven value of problems
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as a significant mathematical question is often a matter of taste; if AI makes some problems easy, mathematicians may devalue them and shift to other questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of mathematical work should include judgments of importance and novelty, recognizing that community values and fashions influence which results are considered meaningful. The article emphasizes that ease of solution (via AI) can change perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of subject areas for automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fields are more amenable to automation — e.g., optimization, combinatorics, and areas relying on symbolic representations like algebra — while others may be harder for AI to fully automate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of whether AI can replace human labor should consider technical character of the field: repetitiveness, symbolic structure, and reliance on large factual knowledge make a subject likelier to be automated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of exploratory, experimental computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using AI to explore large landscapes of problems (e.g., Tao’s project: assessing 22 million possible implications) as preliminary experiments can guide human researchers to promising directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploratory computational output (even if low-quality) is valuable as a heuristic guide: it is judged useful when it surfaces directions for deeper human-led work rather than being taken as final proof or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human creativity: new definitions, abstractions, and research direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if AI proves many statements, humans are expected to continue to provide the fundamental creative work: devising new definitions, abstractions, and selecting important research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames such high-level, conceptual contributions as enduringly valuable criteria for judging mathematical work; novelty of perspective and conceptual framing remain central human metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment moderation standards for the article’s discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Quanta Magazine moderates comments to facilitate an informed, substantive, civil conversation. Abusive, profane, self-promotional, misleading, incoherent or off-topic comments will be rejected. Moderators are staffed during regular business hours (New York time) and can only accept comments written in English.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational rules for public discussion: enforce civility, topicality, non-commercial content, clarity, and English language; moderation occurs within stated staffing constraints.
